source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
Georgia has 49 mapped data center facilities and only 5 publish a megawatt figure, so the state's AI power footprint is mostly unmetered in public.

That gap is the pattern worth holding onto. A facility can be mapped, named, and ranked while its actual electrical load stays undisclosed. Microsoft's Fulton County campus is exactly that case: 489,370 square feet of technical space is the only published specification, and it carries no megawatt figure, no rack count, and no accelerator count. Square footage is real, but it converts to capacity only through a density assumption the operator has not stated, so no rack or load estimate for this campus can be derived from the record.

For AI specifically, this matters because the binding constraint on scaling is power and the buildings that deliver it, not floor area. A training campus and a colocation hall can occupy similar square footage and draw vastly different loads from the grid. Without a published megawatt figure, a reader cannot tell which one this is, and cannot connect the building to the power constraint that governs whether it can host AI workloads at all.

What the data does not cover is equally important. It does not say how much power this campus draws, whether it is built out or partially occupied, or what hardware it holds. The state ranking that places this campus sixth by published megawatt cannot be reconciled with the campus page, because the campus page publishes no megawatt figure. Any capacity number attached to this site by anyone else is an estimate, not a disclosure.
